newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW-Japan Nov customs-cleared trade data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Japan Nov customs-cleared trade data.

text.p: The following is a selection of analysts' reactions to Japan's customs-cleared trade data for November released on Wednesday, which showed a year-on-year rise of 0.2 percent to 675.19 billion yen.
RICHARD JERRAM, ING BARING SECURITIES, TOKYO:

"It's a quite surprise. It's the first increase in the surplus for two years. It's certainly higher than we expected. Certainly, if anything, it shows the trade surplus is going to be turning around earlier than we expected."

"Obviously U.S. car makers are becoming a little bit nervous with the weakening of the yen and are probably suffering from a loss of competitiveness. At the moment there doesn't seem to be any great pressure (for the U.S.) to take out a big stick and beat Japan on trade, but if the surplus keeps on going up, I'm sure in the new year you will see a more aggressive stance.

"I think the crucial thing (for currency levels) is what's going to happen to the direction of the Japanese surplus and what is going to happen in the U.S. if and when interest rates increase... I would have thought the yen will turn around in the middle of the next calender year."
"The U.S. government will start applying some pressure on the Japanese...so the yen's basic trend will be stronger than current level, that means, maybe below 110 yen.

"The effect of (increased) Japanese exports is beginning to appear due to the sharp depreciation of the yen... The time is coming for us to see a bottoming-out period of the Japanese trade surplus. In the near future, the trend will be an increase in the Japanese surplus against the U.S."

"I doubt if Japan's trade surplus will keep rising, as the rise in the November surplus appeared to be caused by such a temporary factor as an increase in car exports to the United States. There is a possibility that the surplus will show a decline again. There will not be a change in the business structure of Japanese companies in which they have shifted production abroad. The yen's depreciation looks like beefing up the competitive edge of Japanese exporters."
